neighbours.label: a structure raised / built / standing 'on' a solid supporting base (stilts, slab, pedestal, piers): fires on ' on' and the words leading into the base noun
fire: The fishing huts along the estuary are raised on wooden piles driven deep into the mud.
The new garage was built on a concrete pad that had cured for three weeks.
The bronze horse stands on a marble plinth at the entrance to the park.
Most of the old granaries in the region are raised on stone piers to keep out the rats.
The bungalow was erected on a reinforced concrete raft because the soil was so soft.
The lighthouse stands on a granite ledge a mile off the coast.
The whole village is elevated on stilts above the tidal flats.
The memorial obelisk was set on a concrete footing two metres square.
quiet: The fishing huts along the estuary were painted bright red by their owners every spring.
The new garage was designed by an architect who had cured his fear of heights.
The bronze horse was stolen from the entrance to the park and never seen again.
Most of the old granaries in the region were abandoned after the rats arrived.
The vines climb up a wire lattice strung between two tall poles.
The lighthouse keeper rowed a mile out from the coast every single morning.
The whole village gathers beside the tidal flats to watch the boats come in.
The marquee has a light aluminium frame with a canvas roof stretched over it.

notes: Card: ' on', ' a', ' small', ' large', ' concrete' before slab / step / landfill islands / basements; output promotes ' base', ' disk', ' cup', ' pot'. The - pole is the other side: frames, lattices, trellises that things climb or hang on (suppressed here: ' frame', ' scaffold', ' poles'). Probes: raised on stilts 1.26, granite pedestal 0.77, concrete slab 0.66; but 'mounted on a small platform' 0.01 and 'sits on a heavy round base' 0.20, so the label is narrower than 'any base'. Near misses keep the structures and drop the on-a-base relation.
